note:
Trained on synthetic self-labelled data (258 samples, reduced from the spec traffic 8-10k target -- see generate_data.py, itself reduced from a 1215-cell grid to keep local generation time reasonable). Evaluated on a held-out split of the SAME synthetic distribution, NOT the human-written holdout technical.md section 9.3 requires -- that holdout does not exist yet and must come from the team, never from an LLM. These numbers describe how well the model fits its own synthetic distribution, not real-world triage accuracy.

HONEST FINDING from this training run, worth preserving: the spec (section 9.3) prescribes critical x2 weighting in the acuity head loss. At this dataset size, that weighting caused the acuity head to collapse to always predicting critical (macro-F1 stuck at exactly 0.1667 across every epoch, matching the closed-form value for a degenerate all-critical classifier -- confirmed independently via a plain sklearn LogisticRegression probe on frozen embeddings, which hit the same wall, ruling out a training-loop bug). Removing the weight (critical_multiplier=1.0) let both heads learn real, non-degenerate signal, but critical_recall dropped to 0.15 -- i.e. the model catches only ~15% of critical cases on this holdout, which is dangerous for a system whose whole point is not missing critical emergencies. This is a genuine tension the spec does not resolve: the safety-motivated weighting and learnability are in direct conflict at low sample counts. The system-level safety net (rule-based fragility/mlc_flag flags, and the triage-unavailable fallback in core/app/integrations/ml/intake.py defaulting to acuity=critical) is what actually protects against missed critical cases right now, NOT this model. Do not treat this checkpoint as safe to run without that fallback active. Real fix: scale generate_data.py to the spec target (8-10k samples, ideally via Kaggle for the compute budget) and re-tune the critical weight once there is enough data per class for it to do its intended job instead of degenerating.
also_tried_mean_pooling_vs_cls: mean-pooling over tokens beat [CLS] pooling by a wide margin (facility macro-F1 0.156 vs 0.023 in the diagnostic probe) -- MuRIL is a plain MLM, never trained with [CLS] as a sentence embedding the way SBERT-style models are. Applied to the real model.
